title: Prepositions that come after
goal: Use eight Urdu postpositions, and put nouns into the oblique form that must go with them — a pattern you'll meet in every sentence until the last unit.
bekal: use میں، پر، سے، کو، تک، کے ساتھ، کے لیے، کے پاس
change nouns to the oblique form before a postposition
talk about directions and places around town

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — رکشے میں
dialogs.intro: Budi stands at the roadside and flags down an auto-rickshaw. The driver turns around.

notes: **Every Urdu "preposition" comes after the noun.** "In Lahore" is لاہور میں, literally "Lahore in". "From Indonesia" is انڈونیشیا سے. That's why they're called **postpositions**, not prepositions. Nothing exotic about it — Japanese, Korean, and Turkish work exactly the same way, and after two weeks your ear stops fighting it.

**A postposition pulls its noun into the oblique form.** The word لڑکا becomes لڑکے کو, and کمرا becomes کمرے میں. Only masculine nouns ending in ـا change in the singular; the rest stay put. But **every** plural noun changes to ـوں — لڑکوں کو · کتابوں میں · گھروں میں.

**Compound postpositions start with کے.** کے پاس (near, have), کے ساتھ (with), کے لیے (for), کے بعد (after), کے پہلے (before), کے پیچھے (behind), کے سامنے (in front of), کے بارے میں (about). They all use کے, which is why pronouns change: میرے پاس, not میرا پاس.

**The word کوئی means "someone" and also "some, a".** The question کوئی اور ہے؟ = "is anyone else there?". The phrase کوئی کتاب = "some book". With نہیں it becomes "not a single one": کوئی بات نہیں ("no problem"), کوئی مسئلہ نہیں ("no trouble at all"). For things, the better word is کچھ (*kuchh*): کچھ اور؟ ("anything else?").

**Addressing someone whose name you don't know.** The phrase بھائی صاحب ("brother, sir") works for any man your age or older: drivers, vendors, clerks. For women: باجی or آپا. For people much older: انکل and آنٹی — two English words that have become fully Urdu and aren't the least bit impolite.

**The word چلیں is the invitation you'll hear most.** It means "let's go", "come on", "well then". Its cousins are چلو (casual) and چلیے (polite). At the end of a phone call, اچھا چلیں means "OK, that's it for now".

grammars.title: Eight postpositions that cover A1
body: Learn these eight along with their examples, and you can build almost every sentence about place, time, and purpose you need at this level.

head: Postposition
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: بازار تک — as far as the bazaar
دوست کے ساتھ — with a friend

after: ⚠️ The postposition سے does three jobs that English splits between three words: "from" (لاہور سے), "with" for a tool (قلم سے لکھنا, to write with a pen), and "than" in comparisons (اس سے بڑا, bigger than that — unit 19). Don't be surprised to find it in unexpected places.

grammars.title: The oblique form: what changes and what doesn't
body: As soon as a postposition attaches, the noun in front of it goes into the **oblique form**. For most nouns the oblique singular is identical to the ordinary form — so there are really only two rows you need to remember.
after: Pronouns have their own oblique forms, and these are the ones you'll use most: the word میں becomes مجھ · the word تم stays تم · the word آپ stays آپ · the word یہ becomes اس · the word وہ becomes اس · the word ہم stays ہم · and plural وہ becomes ان. So "to me" is مجھ کو — which is then shortened to مجھے, and the short form is what people actually say.
Adjectives ending in ـا go oblique too: بڑا کمرا becomes بڑے کمرے میں ("in the big room"). Feminine adjectives, and adjectives that don't end in ـا, never change at all.

blocks.title: Three sentences that will save you on the street
items: Asking the way: معاف کیجیے، بازار کہاں ہے؟ ("Excuse me, where's the bazaar?"). To be more precise: یہاں سے کتنی دور ہے؟ ("how far is it from here?").

Haggling over a rickshaw fare: بھائی صاحب، تھوڑا کم کیجیے ("brother, bring it down a little"). Bargaining is normal and expected in Pakistan, but keep it light — never demanding. Once the price is right: ٹھیک ہے، چلیں.

Giving up politely when you don't understand: معاف کیجیے، میں سمجھا نہیں (male speaker) or میں سمجھی نہیں (female speaker) — "sorry, I didn't understand". Follow it with آہستہ بولیے ("please speak slowly"), and Pakistanis almost always will.

بازار ____ کتنے پیسے؟ (as far as the bazaar)
میرے ____ وقت نہیں ہے۔ (I don't have time)
